sentences.text: Teleocrater was a carnivorous quadruped measuring 7 to 10 feet in length, distinguished by unusually long neck vertebrae with unique cervical neural canal openings that transition from wider-than-tall at the front to taller-than-wide at the back of the neck.
The genus name Teleocrater refers to its mostly closed acetabulum, or hip socket, while its scapula socket is oriented downwards and backwards more than in the related genus Yarasuchus.

The lack of preserved osteoderms suggests Teleocrater probably did not have them, unlike many pseudosuchians, and its hindlimb proportions resemble silesaurids and pseudosuchians rather than running lineages, as its metatarsus is not lengthened relative to the femur and tibia.
Its fibula features a long twisted crest for muscle attachment and an expanded front edge at the top.
Teleocrater is the oldest known bird-line archosaur, predating the previous record holder, Asilisaurus.
Fossil evidence suggests Teleocrater was transported by several floods before burial, as its smaller bones are more fragmented than those of larger contemporaries.
The holotype specimen of Teleocrater was discovered by Francis Rex Parrington in 1933 near the village of Mkongoleko in the Ruhuhu Basin of southern Tanzania.
Alan J. Charig first described the remains of Teleocrater in his 1956 PhD thesis, though the name was coined in that doctoral dissertation but was not formally published at that time.
The genus and species were formally named and described in a 2017 study published in Nature, officially published in 2017 by Sterling Nesbitt and colleagues.
A bonebed containing at least three individuals was discovered in 2015 within 1 km of the original discovery site, and newer specimens of Teleocrater come from Bonebed Z183.
A preserved tooth that is compressed, recurved, and serrated on both edges indicates Teleocrater was carnivorous.

Teleocrater's hindlimbs were not adapted for running, as its metatarsal bones were not elongated like those of running lineages, and its hindlimb proportions resemble silesaurids and pseudosuchians rather than running lineages, as its metatarsus is not lengthened relative to the femur and tibia.

Bone histology shows Teleocrater had moderately fast growth rates, similar to ornithodirans rather than crocodilians, and the cortical bone of Teleocrater was thin, measuring approximately 1 to 1.5 mm thick. Histological evidence indicates that Teleocrater specimens were growing rapidly when they died, and its growth rate was faster than basal archosaurs and similar to silesaurids, but slower than Nyasasaurus, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs.
The only known species of the genus is Teleocrater rhadinus, and it is classified within the unranked family Aphanosauria, where the parent group of the genus Teleocrater is Aphanosauria.

Phylogenetic analysis places Teleocrater within the group Aphanosauria, closely related to Yarasuchus, Dongusuchus, and Spondylosoma, and the Aphanosauria group includes Yarasuchus but excludes birds and crocodiles. Research indicates Teleocrater is closely related to the problematic genera Dongusuchus and Yarasuchus, which are also aphanosaurs.
The Aphanosauria group is the sister group to Ornithodira, which includes dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
A 2008 histological study tentatively identified Teleocrater as an archosauromorph closely related to, but not included in, the family Erythrosuchidae.

Teleocrater lived during the Middle Triassic period in the Manda Formation of Tanzania, specifically during the Anisian epoch of the Triassic period within the Middle Triassic of Tanzania within the Manda Formation.
The phylogenetic placement of Scleromochlus varies between datasets, though it is consistently recovered as an avemetatarsalian.
